Recent findings suggest that wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Recent findings suggest that aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

According to recent reports, baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

It has been revealed that did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar challenges).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

It has been revealed that onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

In a recent development, thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

According to recent reports, peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

In a recent development, another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Industry observers note that witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

According to recent reports, blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Recent findings suggest that though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Recent findings suggest that using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Sources indicate that ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That mentioned, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food.

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

Sources indicate that L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:.

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:.

Recent findings suggest that L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

According to recent reports, L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.).

Recent findings suggest that and though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.).

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:.

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Industry observers note that research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

Photography by Daniel Reiser.

The UK’s Royal Society for Arts has declared five Royal Designers for Industry, who include Durrell Bishop and Bridget Baines, as well as naming an Honorary Royal Designer as it celebrates its 90th anniversary.

Industry observers note that the awards, which were established in 1936, recognise outstanding talent across landscape architecture, technology, illustration, fashion and theatre. They are given by Royal Society for Arts (RSA) and can only be held by 200 designers at any one time.

This year’s winners are product and interaction designer Bishop, multidisciplinary designer Harris Elliott, illustrator Laura Carlin, costume designer Tahra Zafar and landscape architect Bridget Baines.

Baines co-founded international practice Gross Max, and her fellow Gross Max founder Eelco Hooftman (pictured in main image with Baines) was given the Honorary Royal Designer award this year.

The winners were chosen for their “joyful” designs,.

In a recent development, “Ninety years on, the Royal Designers are still looking forward,” Keeper of the Faculty of Royal Designers for Industry Johanna Gibbons stated. “This year’s appointments show how far design now reaches, from public landscapes and picture books to exhibitions, the stage and the objects we use every day.”.

It has been revealed that “Their work is joyful, and it is serious about making life better,” she continued. “That is what unites Royal Designers across the decades: a living entanglement of disciplines that, with the RSA Fellowship, is a profound force for good.”.

Last year’s winners included designer Yinka Ilori and journalist Mona Chalabi, and the award has also been given to designers including Es Devlin, Vivienne Westwood, James Dyson and Zandra Rhodes.

According to the RSA, the winners represent the “sheer breadth of design today”.

“Great design changes how we experience the world, often in ways we barely notice,” RSA programme manager Catherine Joyce.

“For 90 years, Royal Designers have shown what extraordinary creativity can achieve, and how it can make life better for everyone,” she continued.“These six appointments are a wonderful reminder of the sheer breadth of design today.”.

Dezeen also recently celebrated the best designers of this year as part of our Dezeen Awards, including Ilori, Yasmine Ghoniem and Keiji Ashizawa.

Photography by Daniel Reiser.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After picking up the 2025 Calder Prize, the multidisciplinary Tokyo-based Yuko Mohri artist has been on a recent roll, opening institutional shows from Santander in Spain and her first US solo show in Miami Beach to bringing her 2024 Venice Biennale presentation home to her native Japan.
  • Among the highlights is In Concert (until 24 January 2027), her solo exhibition at the Barbican Centre’s The Curve gallery in London.
  • The Art Newspaper: How did your Barb­ican residency come about?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After picking up the 2025 Calder Prize, the multidisciplinary Tokyo-based Yuko Mohri artist has been on a recent roll, opening institutional shows from Santander in Spain and her first US solo show in Miami Beach to bringing her 2024 Venice Biennale presentation home to her native Japan.

Among the highlights is In Concert (until 24 January 2027), her solo exhibition at the Barbican Centre’s The Curve gallery in London. At the show’s core is a series of site-responsive kinetic and sound installations made with objects she found at the Barbican. These objects, either stored away or nearly tossed out, embed the history and memories of this famed cultural centre, which will be closed for a year from June 2028 for a £191m revamp ahead of its 50th anniversary in 2032. According to Mohri, the pieces represent an ongoing process that may lead to imperfection, which she finds more profound than a picture-perfect scenario.

The Art Newspaper: How did your Barb­ican residency come about?

Yuko Mohri: When I was approached for a project at The Curve, I discussed with Inês Geraldes Cardoso, the curator of this exhibition, the possibility of researching the Barbican Centre.

The Curve is a unique and challenging space, and they accept experimental projects with artists. I am not the kind of artist who needs to work within a white cube. I understand why they chose me to create something unique. I am, however, the kind of artist who needs time to understand the environment and identify interesting elements that already exist in that context. A research residency is necessary.

In a recent development, but rather than focusing on just this curved gallery space, I wanted to see what the Barbican really is. It is a huge centre involving many different departments and activities. Thousands of people are also living here in the attached residential complex.

After rounds of negotiations, I was offered a two-week residency to look for objects and meet the people living and working here. I got a temporary studio at The Pit, a small theatre space located in the basement.

In a recent development, “Imperfection is everywhere,” Yuko Mohri says. “It’s a great element.” Photo: © Toby Coulson/Barbican Centre.

What were your biggest discoveries?

The centre has many departments, but they seem very separate from each other and don’t have a lot of communication between them. But since they are going to have a major renovation, they want to revamp the centre’s system, too, and strengthen communication.

Recent findings suggest that we started researching different departments and looked for objects across all the spaces. I wanted to collect objects from here that resonate with the space.

In a recent development, among the most iconic ones are the original Barbican lamps featured throughout this exhibition. These were once used as street lamps surrounding the centre and also in the building. But as time went on, they were replaced with those of a upcoming design. They were dusty and strange, but I immediately knew that I wanted to use them for my installation. So I spent a lot of time washing these lamps in my temporary studio.

In a recent development, the speakers that I use for the newly introduced iteration of the ongoing Decomposition series (begun 2021) located near the entrance to The Curve are old speakers from the Barbican. The found cables that I use to connect the fruit with the lamps and the sound are also very important to me. I also found these metal junk pieces that were discarded in a workshop, and I reappropriated them as triggers for the lamps in the installations in the middle part of the exhibition.

In a recent development, throughout this project I met many people outside the gallery space, from engineers to the caretakers of the parking space. The extensive communication helped me connect with a lot of open-minded people who accept me and my work.

Yuko Mohri’s Moré Moré (Leaky) is an ongoing installation inspired by the water leaks at Tokyo metro stations Photo: Sun Shi; courtesy the artist, Project Fulfill Art Space, mother’s tankstation, Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tanya Bonakdar Gallery and WHITE SPACE.

How do you relate the centre’s characteristics with your practice?

The Barbican has many water leaks. There’s also a leak of sound because The Curve wraps around the concert hall. So these leaky elements resonate with my practice, especially my ongoing Moré Moré (Leaky) series (begun 2017), which was inspired by the water leaks at Tokyo metro stations and how the staff contain these water leaks with temporary fixes using everyday items. I presented a version of this in Venice.

This time at the Barbican, I created a large-scale installation located towards the exit of The Curve, using found objects such as a pot, an umbrella, plastic bottles, Wellington boots, traffic cones and old water sinks designed for the Barbican apartments.

Recent findings suggest that I also keep the space open and transparent by removing the covers on the entrances and the back so that people can see what’s going on there from the outside. I also exposed the inner layers of the walls to give people a peek into what is behind them.

Are you building an ecosystem within the Barbican that makes the inaudible heard and the invisible seen?

According to recent reports, instead of building, I see it as repairing. Inspired by attending concert rehearsals at the Barbican, I chose the title In Concert, which mirrors the Latin root consertare. It carries the meaning of repair and adjustment, resembling the process of making an organisation.

The process is also similar to making an installation. When I started, I had no idea how it would turn out eventually. I constantly make adjustments to the elements of my installations, like a conductor making adjustments to the tempo or the volume of the musical instruments. The title also reflects that what you see is not stable. Water leaks, gravity and the audience’s presence will change even some very tiny elements. It is not a finalised show. It’s an ongoing process.

Would you say that you are in control and at the same time you also let go?

I am a human being and I have a desire for a certain outcome. But somehow, it doesn’t always work. This trial and error process is a very learnable process for me.

We all have our expectations, but our society and environment have become increasingly unstable. For example, this summer Tokyo rained non-stop for a record 36 consecutive days. We need to adjust our lives. It’s also a necessity when we are based in Tokyo, constantly facing natural disasters like earthquakes. Japan has long been isolated, but now we have many immigrants. Our society is changing. I see this as a kind of training and accept these changing forces. It’s not necessarily about making things perfect. Imperfection is everywhere. It is a great element.

An edition of Mohri’s ongoing installation Decomposition from 2022 in Kanazawa, Japan Photo: Yuu Takagi; courtesy the artist, Project Fulfill Art Space, mother’s tankstation, Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tanya Bonakdar Gallery and WHITE SPACE.

Education: 2004 BFA, Tama Art University; 2006 MFA, Tokyo University of the Arts.

Key highlights: 2026 The Bass, Miami Beach; 2026 Yokohama Museum of Art; 2026 Centro Botín, Santander; 2025 Pirelli HangarBicocca, Milan; 2024 Japan Pavilion, Venice Biennale; 2023 14th Gwangju Biennale.

Represented by: Tanya Bonakdar Gallery, Upcoming York; Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tokyo; Mother’s Tankstation, London; White Space, Beijing; Project Fulfill Art Space, Taipei.

• Yuko Mohri: In Concert, Barbican Centre, London, until 24 January 2027.

#161537. Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2104 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that by now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy.
  • Industry observers note that at present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll.
  • In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that by now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

Industry observers note that at present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting people’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

In a recent development, some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

According to recent reports, on top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He says this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

On top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

It has been revealed that “We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” claims Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”.

According to recent reports, sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

“During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu states. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

Sources indicate that in general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu notes. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

But GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, states Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.).

At the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu says losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

Industry observers note that as mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

Recent findings suggest that “Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she indicates. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

It’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying challenges may benefit sexual health.

That means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

In a recent development, “Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he indicates. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.).

GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, claims Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

Finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, says board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

According to recent reports, of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

Sources indicate that in a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist customers stated the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

It has been revealed that “Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he indicates. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”.

For those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon notes. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

According to recent reports, in these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

Recent findings suggest that “Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer states. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”.

Desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer indicates. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Sexual health, Dr. Dovec says, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”.

If you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

According to recent reports, working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

According to recent reports, inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

It has been revealed that nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

It has been revealed that grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Recent findings suggest that grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or complications with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

It has been revealed that so, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:.

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

Industry observers note that if your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

In a recent development, for some newly introduced parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

It has been revealed that remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:.

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

Industry observers note that these devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

In a recent development, it involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Whether you're a musician who needs accurate monitoring, a designer who wants something better than AirPods for long editing sessions, or simply someone who loves quality audio, Linsoul IEMs make some of the best IEMs (in-ear-monitors) around.

But, other than the best budget IEMs, they usually don't come cheap, so when Black Friday comes around, it's the perfect time to pick up a bargain.

Industry observers note that in this article, I've picked out the IEMs I think are most worth your money, running from budget single-driver sets to the best multi-driver IEMs under $500. Many are models I've tested myself, and all of them punch well above their price tags.

Sources indicate that I just love this IEM. Billed as the world's flattest IEM, the Reference is built for people who want to hear exactly what's on the recording. Twin 10mm dynamic drivers in a horizontally opposed layout handle the bass, while two Sonion balanced armatures take the mids and a Knowles supertweeter covers the top end. It's the top pick in my best IEMs under $500 guide for a good reason.

This is Xenns Mangird's most premium IEM to date, and it doesn't hold back on hardware: two dynamic drivers and eight balanced armatures per side, split across a four-way crossover. As a result, you get to enjoy a wide, open soundstage with clear, airy treble and loads of detail, while the swirling, abalone-style resin faceplates mean that no two pairs look quite the same.

Recent findings suggest that I'm a significant fan of the Tea Pro, which I called "engagingly musical and beautifully built" in my review. Its dual 8mm dynamic drivers and six balanced armatures deliver a full, natural and lush sound, with a sub-bass presence that's always there without ever swamping the midrange. It's not the most analytical, but perfect to relax into for hours at a time.

Industry observers note that on a tighter budget? The EW300 packs a lot of tech for the cash, combining three driver types in one compact CNC-machined shell: a 10mm dynamic driver for the bass and mids, plus a 6mm planar and a piezoelectric driver working together on the highs. Swappable nozzles let you tweak the tuning, and overall, the sound from this IEM is warm, punchy and forgiving.

Sources indicate that out of all of ZiiGaat's recent releases, the Horizon is my favourite, earning 8 out of 10 in my review. It pairs a 10mm dynamic driver with two Knowles balanced armatures and two planar drivers, producing a bright-leaning, detailed sound with an impressively spacious soundstage. If you can handle a lively treble, it's an absolute treat.

According to recent reports, launched in 2022, the original Cadenza is a bit of a legend, and it's still the perfect budget entry point into the world of IEMs. A single 10mm beryllium diaphragm dynamic driver, sat inside a 3D-printed resin shell, delivers a balanced sound with rich mids and clear treble, for a low, low price. Light, comfortable and a major step up from basic buds.

Released early this year, the Cadenza II builds on its predecessor with a upcoming 10mm titanium-coated dynamic driver and Kiwi Ears' updated KARS 2.0 bass-tuning system. My review focused on its near-neutral sound and excellent build quality, which includes a CNC-machined aluminium faceplate. If you like your sound bass-heavy, look elsewhere, but if you seek an affordable all-rounder, you're golden.

According to recent reports, billed as the world's first MEMS + 1DD + 3BA tribrid IEM, the Halcyon pairs a MEMS driver, a type of tech also used in hearing aids, with a 10mm dynamic driver and three balanced armatures. When testing it for my review I loved its deep, rumbly sub-bass and well-judged treble; if your playlists lean bass-heavy, it really shines.

Sources indicate that the Odyssey pairs a custom 10mm dynamic driver with three genuine Knowles balanced armatures: two full-range drivers for the mids and an ultra-high frequency tweeter. What makes it stand out is its bass: low notes hit like a subwoofer but stop promptly rather than lingering. That keeps the neutral midrange clean and uncluttered, with vocals that sound natural rather than plasticky.

According to recent reports, this IEM is a collab between audio brand ZiiGaat and YouTube reviewer Zeos of Z Reviews. Its single 10mm diamond-like carbon (DLC) dynamic driver serves up a hefty 16dB bass shelf, with warm, rich mids and enough treble extension to stop things getting muddy. If you like your music to rumble, this is the one.

The Lush is ZiiGaat's take on a studio monitor and is designed for sound engineers and stage musicians. It pairs a 10mm dynamic driver with four balanced armatures via a three-way crossover, with the bass cut off at 200Hz so it doesn't bleed into the mids. Expect a neutral, coherent and versatile sound in a light, comfortable resin shell.

As the name suggests, Punch Audio is all about big, bold bass, and the Patada gives that tradition a refined twist. Combining a 10mm ceramic diaphragm dynamic driver with a MEMS driver for the top end makes for a smoother, more open treble than you might expect, alongside the usual low-end thump. This is still a basshead set, then, just a slightly more well-behaved one.

The KE4 uses two 10mm dynamic drivers in an isobaric subwoofer arrangement, paired with two balanced armatures through a three-way crossover. It was an early affordable take on the 'Upcoming Meta' tuning, and when I reviewed it, I found the bass hefty but the midrange the real star: rich, layered and never boxy or thin. It's comfortable and non-fatiguing to wear, too.

Industry observers note that crinEar's first production IEM, the Daybreak, arrived in 2025 and is built more for enjoyment than analysis. Its combines a dynamic driver, two balanced armatures and two micro-planar drivers in a 3D-printed resin shell with aluminium faceplates. If the Reference prioritises strict accuracy, the Daybreak goes for a more engaging, crowd-pleasing sound that works with pretty much any genre.

It's been a remarkable year for in-ear monitors, and Chinese brands, often lumped together under the "ChiFi "label, are a big reason why. Companies such as ZiiGaat, Kiwi Ears and Simgot are releasing fresh models at a dizzying pace, and they're no longer just competing on price.

We're seeing genuine innovation, from MEMS drivers to micro-planars, alongside a wave of collaborations with influential reviewers such as Z Reviews and HBB.

The upshot? Sound quality that would have cost a small fortune a decade ago is now available for less than a decent pair of trainers, and the gap with the big established brands keeps on shrinking.

Industry observers note that beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. As Ecom Editor on Creative Bloq, when he's not reviewing the latest audiophile headphones or evaluating the best designed ergonomic office chairs, he’s testing laptops, TVs and monitors, all so he can find the best tech deals for Creative Bloq’s digital professional audience.

#161534. What Is ‘Nonnamaxxing’? The Italian Grandma Lifestyle Might Be the Secret to Longevity

What Is ‘Nonnamaxxing’? The Italian Grandma Lifestyle Might Be the Secret to Longevity

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1522 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live.
  • I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a new wellness trend making the rounds on social media.
  • Sources indicate that there’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live. They walk everywhere, frequently across the city, without any assistance. Many of them are dressed to the nines, but they also don’t try to hide their age.

I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a new wellness trend making the rounds on social media. “Nonnamaxxing” is the idea that anyone can maximize their life if they just embrace the habits of Italian grandmas. It happens to be sensible guidance.

Sources indicate that there’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers. Italy leads the European Union in life expectancy, and it’s a country where the number of centenarians is growing. A cluster of villages in Sardinia is one of the world’s five Blue Zones. Online guidance includes ditching social media, eating homemade everything, wearing cotton nightgowns, and welcoming unhurried lunches with friends. Some of these suggestions line up with how I’ve seen Italian grandmas live. But as a health and science journalist, I’ve noticed there’s more to it than what looks good on Instagram or TikTok. In fact, Licia Fertz, a 96-year-old Italian nonna based in Viterbo, Italy, tells SELF, quite the opposite is true.

“I put on my makeup and dress in cheerful colors, even if I’m not leaving the house, because presenting yourself well is an act of self-love,” Fertz indicates.

Industry observers note that it seems that Italian nonne are the health gurus we all need. Read on to learn their secrets to a happier, healthier, and longer life.

According to recent reports, I rarely see Italian nonne who don’t look their age. In fact, it’s one of the first things I noticed when I moved here. At the pools and beaches, it doesn’t matter how old they are; women, nonne included, frequently wear bikinis. Honestly, it’s refreshing and emphasizes a cultural mindset that aging is a natural part of life.

Fertz tells SELF that this mindset is key to her living a long and healthy life. “Never think of yourself as old,” says Fertz. “You are born young.”.

It turns out that as you age, having a more positive attitude about getting older could help you live longer too. A recent study found an association between how women view aging and the actual pace at which they age.

Industry observers note that sonja Lyubomirsky, a distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and author of How To Feel Loved, tells SELF that a mindset is like putting on a pair of glasses or a coat. “It certainly matters very much what our mindset is when we think about aging,” Lyubomirsky notes. “Is it a gift? Is it about wisdom, maturity, and the richness of life, or is it about deterioration and loss?” Both can be true, she says. “But you can choose.”.

At school pick-up for my daughter, I don’t only see other parents. I also see Italian nonne. That’s because Italian grandmas are very involved in their grandkids’ lives and take an active role in caregiving. In fact, for better or worse, the Italian economy is supported by the unpaid labor of Italian grandmothers—and this is well-known and discussed in local mom groups.

Recent findings suggest that research indicates that caregiving later in life may lead to better aging and act as a buffer against cognitive decline. One recent study found that grandparents who provided childcare—ranging from caring for sick grandkids, helping with homework, or driving them to school—scored higher on memory and verbal fluency tests compared with those who didn’t help with childcare.

“I live with my grandson,” Fertz tells SELF. “I’m a great-grandmother, and every day spent with my great-granddaughter is a gift that never ceases to amaze me.”.

According to recent reports, even if you’re not a grandparent, helping others can yield similar health benefits. According to research published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, people who volunteered more than 100 hours a year—versus those who volunteered zero hours a year—had a reduced risk of mortality, more optimism, and purpose in their lives.

Industry observers note that italian cities and villages are highly walkable, meaning walking isn’t something people do for exercise; it’s just a way of life. Even if someone has a car, sometimes a destination is only reachable by foot because Italy’s infamously narrow streets. Gas is also more expensive in Italy. While this might be inconvenient for some, a walking-first lifestyle happens to be associated with longevity.

“Walking is the most fundamental form of human physical activity and many, many hundreds of studies confirm that walking helps people age slower and better,” Daniel Lieberman, a professor of Human Evolutionary Biology at Harvard University, tells SELF. “Walking helps you age well.”.

Industry observers note that paola Mariotti, a pediatrician and nonna based in Florence, Italy, tells SELF that walking is very important to her, and was very important to her own grandparents, who didn’t have a car and walked everywhere. Today, as a more modern nonna, Mariotti focuses on walking at least 5,000 steps a day—which she tracks on her phone—but strives to get 10,000 steps or more, if possible, each day.

Much of America isn’t walkable, but a 2025 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that even 15 minutes of fast walking a day can reduce premature death.

According to recent reports, at cafés in Italy, I’m always struck by how Italian nonne drink un caffè. Usually, she is just enjoying her coffee and watching people walk by, rather than scrolling on her phone or sending emails on her laptop. Some might call this the dolce far niente, which means the sweetness of doing nothing. While it’s true that these moments of pause and presence are more common in Italy, there’s something deeper to them. They reflect how, as a culture, Italians are content to live more mindfully. They appreciate quality over quantity and don’t feel the need to constantly multitask for the sake of being productive.

In fact, Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist in Newly introduced York, tells SELF that he thinks nonnamaxxing has less to do with actual Italian grandmothers and more about Gen Z’s desire to escape hustle culture. “The appeal here is the fantasy of a life that feels grounded, warm, and unhurried,” Alpert notes. “A lot of younger people are burned out by the pressure to constantly optimize themselves, be productive, and turn their lives into content.”.

While in the moment, multitasking can feel like you’re being more efficient, researchers say that it actually does the opposite and can lead to increased stress levels.

Sources indicate that the antidote to hustle culture is a mindful one. This can be as simple as just enjoying a coffee without much else, as it’s been found that people who stay in the present moment age better and with more resilience.

Sources indicate that in Italy, there’s an emphasis on eating what’s in season. In fact, my local market provides customers with a chart that identifies exactly what fruits and vegetables are in season each month. This lifestyle isn’t exactly optional—produce that’s out-of-season is harder to come by. Antonino De Lorenzo, professor emeritus of human nutrition at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, tells SELF that the value isn’t in the variety of food, but in what’s gained when you choose seasonal produce, which is food that is less likely to have preservatives and industrial products.

Industry observers note that “Freshness, variety, ripeness, and preparation methods can all exert a significant influence on a food’s nutritional profile,” De Lorenzo states. “A high-quality diet, maintained over time, promotes healthier aging, characterized by better preservation of physical, mental, and cognitive functions, as well as reduced exposure to major chronic diseases.”.

It has been revealed that indeed, the Mediterranean diet, which focuses on olive oil, vegetables, fruits, whole grains and legumes—all popular in Italy—has been linked to longevity. As researchers tend to emphasize, the Mediterranean diet isn’t a fad diet. It’s a way of life.

Italian grandmas are stereotypically known for being connected to their communities and neighbors—maybe even a bit too much, in the sense that it can veer into nosiness. Viral videos on social media have joked that Italian nonne are Italy’s security systems.

Recent findings suggest that “The most crucial thing for living a long and happy life? Don’t isolate yourself,” Fertz says. “Always stay in touch with people, travel, blueprint outings, and get out of the house.”.

According to a study in The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, having a sense of purpose can help preserve cognitive function as you age. A separate study found that people with a higher sense of purpose had a reduced risk for depression and loneliness. Whether that is being in-the-know in your community, or finding a hobby to keep you busy, the key is to feel connected and busy.

Because boredom, Fertz claims, is “the one thing that truly makes you old.”.

Brussels’s expansive, €230m Kanal art complex set to open in former Citroën garage

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The much-anticipated Kanal, billed in press materials as Europe’s largest museum development, opens tomorrow (28 November) in a former Citroën garage and showroom on the banks of Brussels’s Charleroi–Brussels Canal.
  • The Brussels-Capital Region acquired the site, which dates back to 1934, in 2015 with the intention of creating a major cultural centre.
  • Three upcoming structures, called “houses”, have been inserted into the former garage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The much-anticipated Kanal, billed in press materials as Europe’s largest museum development, opens tomorrow (28 November) in a former Citroën garage and showroom on the banks of Brussels’s Charleroi–Brussels Canal. The institution aims to establish Brussels as a major international centre for Modern and contemporary art, and also to provide newly introduced truly public, inclusive institution for the city’s residents.

The Brussels-Capital Region acquired the site, which dates back to 1934, in 2015 with the intention of creating a major cultural centre. The work was then carried out by an international team featuring noAarchitecten, EM2N and Sergison Bates. The resulting complex spans 40,000 sq. m.

Three upcoming structures, called “houses”, have been inserted into the former garage. Upon entering from the Quai de Willebroeck, visitors find on their left the “Rassembleur”, as the team calls it, which is home to an auditorium and offices. Opposite, on the right, is Kanal Architecture, which is intended to house the CIVA architecture centre and its archives. The transfer of the archives has been delayed following a fire in July. Further along on the right is Kanal-Centre Pompidou, a museum dedicated to modern and contemporary art. This latter space will feature work from the collection of Paris’s Centre Pompidou, with which Kanal signed an agreement in 2017. The agreement, valid until 2031, gives Kanal access to works from the Paris museum's collection, alongside curatorial expertise and support with exhibitions and programming.

Sources indicate that more than 20,000 sq. m within the broader Kanal project is devoted to freely accessible public space. The complex also includes creative studios, observation points, a rooftop bar, a bakery, a restaurant and Carrosserie (French for bodywork), a bistro whose counter is made from shaped car-body sheet metal, finished with a chameleon-effect paint. Work on the site is complete, though construction related to the redevelopment of Place Sainctelette surrounding it is still under way and scheduled to continue until the end of 2027.

In a recent development, the run-up to Kanal’s opening has not been without controversy and challenges. Kanal’s managing director, Yves Goldstein, announced earlier this year that he would step down and he is due to leave his position on Monday (30 November). A statement from the Brussels-Capital Region, the executive body that established the museum, remarked in September: “The parties acknowledge a difference of opinion regarding the future of Kanal.” His replacement is yet to be announced.

Industry observers note that there have meanwhile been years of debate over the institution’s cost, funding and institutional partnerships. The initial investment budget of €150m (€125m for the works and €25m for studies), set out by the Brussels-Capital region in 2017, rose to around €230m. In May 2026, the region granted the Kanal Foundation, established in 2017 to operate the institution, a €60m loan to help complete the construction works and ensure the museum could open as planned. The budget provided for the ongoing operating of the museum, initially projected at €35m a year, was reduced to €28m in 2026 and is projected to fall to €24m in 2027, €22m in 2028 and €10m in 2029. Brussels’ regional government has previously told The Art Newspaper that private investors will be needed from 2028.

The five-year partnership with the Centre Pompidou will cost around €2m a year. Critics have questioned the expense and the decision more generally of partnering with a Paris institution rather than with Brussels-based organisations. Regional politician Benjamin Dalle has described Kanal as a “top-down political project”, arguing that it should have started with local artists and communities. The Fédération des arts plastiques has raised concerns about the place of Belgian artists in the programme, acquisitions and support for emerging practitioners. Kanal has been approached for comment.

It has been revealed that redzisz, however, has defended the museum’s role as a cultural resource for Brussels and its community. “This museum has an obligation to speak as much to locality as to contribute to global debate,” she told The Art Newspaper in October. That approach is reflected in Kanal–Centre Pompidou’s main inaugural exhibition, in which loans from Centre Pompidou mix with others from international institutions as well as works from the Kanal Foundation. The foundation has a particular focus on contemporary artists connected to Belgium—such as Sammy Baloji, Edith Dekyndt and Aglaia Konrad.

In a recent development, the show, titled A Truly Immense Journey, features 350 works across three levels. Marcel Duchamp’s Boîte-en-valise, lent by a Belgian private collector, is placed in dialogue with a version of Alberto Giacometti’s L’Homme qui marche I. Kader Attia’s Untitled (Ghardaïa) (2009), a model of a city made from couscous, borrowed from Tate, is shown alongside two portraits of Leonie Ngoie, a Belgian woman of Congolese descent, photographed by the Belgian artist Chrystel Mukeba against an Art Nouveau backdrop by the Belgian architect and designer Victor Horta.

An installation view of A Truly Immense Journey, featuring 350 works across three levels.

Other exhibitions and projects are spread across the Kanal-Centre Pompidou house. No Show, orchestrated by the Brussels-based artist duo Deborah Bowmann and musician Maoupa Mazzocchetti, brings together around 20 artists from the Belgian capital, all of whom are under 40. Clémentine Deliss’s Department of Traps features 70 objects and paintings, including nets, snares, decoys and trompe-l’œil works, deriving from 11 Brussels museums.

Otobong Nkanga’s installation in Hall 2 encourages audience involvement.

It has been revealed that A key part of the museum’s strategy is to involve the public directly in its programme. The Antwerp-based Nigerian artist Otobong Nkanga, for instance, has created an installation of wooden looms in Hall 2, inviting participants to weave together and contribute to a collective work of art. Nearly 200 pupils from four neighbouring schools have, meanwhile, contributed to writing exhibition labels. “Inclusivity is the best way for the public to make the place their own,” Kasia Redzisz told The Art Newspaper in January.

By 2030, Kanal expects to attract 550,000 visitors a year.

Stranger Than Heaven could be RGG Studio's answer to prestige TV's multilingual period epics

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quick read: Stranger Than Heaven, out 15 January 2027, trades modern Japan for five decades of period crime drama with a multilingual script and a fresh visual style, and it could be RGG Studio's biggest global hit yet.
  • When it comes to capturing contemporary Japan, no studio does it better than RGG Studio and its long-running Yakuza / Like A Dragon series, to the point that players are drawn in not only by its crime-based, melodramatic narrative and surreal side quests, but also by the chance to engage in virtual tourism.
  • Having had the opportunity to play the game from the start at a recent hands-on event, I can say Stranger Than Heaven's story doesn't begin in Japan but in the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quick read: Stranger Than Heaven, out 15 January 2027, trades modern Japan for five decades of period crime drama with a multilingual script and a fresh visual style, and it could be RGG Studio's biggest global hit yet.

When it comes to capturing contemporary Japan, no studio does it better than RGG Studio and its long-running Yakuza / Like A Dragon series, to the point that players are drawn in not only by its crime-based, melodramatic narrative and surreal side quests, but also by the chance to engage in virtual tourism. But its upcoming title, Stranger Than Heaven, marks a departure with a more ambitious vision, taking the player on an epic journey across five decades of early 20th-century Japan.

Having had the opportunity to play the game from the start at a recent hands-on event, I can say Stranger Than Heaven's story doesn't begin in Japan but in the US. While RGG Studio has specialised in making games for a Japanese audience, the past decade has seen Sega make concerted efforts to bring the Yakuza series to a global audience, with 2024's Like A Dragon: Infinite Wealth even largely taking place in Hawaii. Stranger Than Heaven also explores Japan during a period of modernisation and Western influence, as shown through its protagonist, Makoto Daito, an orphan with mixed heritage from America and Japan.

I begin with him fleeing poverty, racial discrimination and cops trying to pin a crime on him, as he stows away on a ship in San Francisco that's bound for Japan, hoping to start a upcoming life - almost like a reverse of the immigrant American Dream narrative.

Sources indicate that in Makoto, we have a young man whose mixed heritage is made clear by his distinct blue eyes, while English is his first language, a radical change from Yakuza's typically middle-aged Japanese characters, which perhaps also reflects the game being developed by a young team, with game director Mikinobu Abe still in his twenties. Not that this was a factor in choosing a younger protagonist, since we'll also follow Makoto as he ages over five decades.

While RGG Studio's characters have always been societal outcasts as part of the criminal underworld, Makoto and another stowaway, Yu Shinjo, have their mixed heritage also single them out in Japan, as passersby don't hesitate to address them as "keto", an ethnic slur against foreigners that literally translates to "hairy barbarian". It's perhaps how he finds a kind of solidarity with the Black smugglers they have stowed away with, whose charismatic leader, Orpheus, is played by none other than Snoop Dogg.

In a recent development, it's a casting choice that reflects Stranger Than Heaven's ambitions to appeal to a global audience, as is the game's theme song with English and Japanese lyrics performed by pop artists Tori Kelly and Ado respectively, who also have roles in the game. What that also means is that rather than having separate language dubs, the game features a single multilingual audio track, putting to bed any 'subs-versus-dubs' debates, while also arriving at a time when multilingual entertainment is getting more mainstream attention, such as the Emmy-winning Shogun.

In a recent development, "This decision was made to authentically portray Makoto’s dual heritage," Abe clarifies. "The narrative centres on the conflicts and challenges that arise from his identity and cultural background." That's something I was also able to appreciate in the game's opening hours set in Kokura, Fukuoka, in 1915, when Makoto is fresh off the boat and, even as someone who doesn't speak the language, I can hear how he is less confident and fluent in Japanese.

Sources indicate that "As the story moves through different eras, Makoto and Yu do not simply grow older; they gradually adapt to life in Japan," Abe explains. "We wanted to express that growth through subtle changes in their body language, mannerisms, and Japanese pronunciation. This meant carefully considering how comfortable they should appear in each scene, so that their adjustment to the environment would feel gradual and natural rather than sudden.".

Recent findings suggest that during my hands-on, I also got to explore a couple of other eras, including Kure, Hiroshima in 1929 and Minami, Osaka in 1943. Notably, the passage of time is not presented in one location but in a latest city each time. While that does follow a geographical trajectory, starting from the South of Japan and working your way across the country until the story culminates in Tokyo in 1965, the cities picked also serve a narrative purpose.

"Kokura was a major industrial city back then, so it felt natural as the destination for someone who had stowed away on a ship," Abe explains. "We chose Kure in 1929 because it is strongly associated in Japan with yakuza stories, most famously through the film Battles Without Honor and Humanity. It has a particular significance for Makoto, who is conflicted over whether he sees himself as Japanese or American, and entering the world of the yakuza - a distinctly Japanese organisation - intensifies that struggle. At the same time, Kure was a major military port with a significant international population, giving Makoto opportunities to encounter people and experiences that reflect another side of his identity.".

With five cities, or rather districts within those cities, it also means a focus on smaller but more densely designed maps closer to Yakuza's Kamurocho compared to the larger, sprawling spaces in the more recent Like A Dragon games.

"Each new city will feel genuinely distinct - not only visually, but also in the way it plays and invites exploration," Abe explains. "Kokura is a dense city where most buildings can be entered, offering players a great deal of depth to explore. Kure is a city built along a coastal mountainside, creating a vertical landscape that encourages exploration across multiple elevations. In Minami, the buildings become taller, and players can enter large multi-tenant complexes.".

Sources indicate that while there is a challenge in depicting the main cast physically ageing across five decades, it's also expressed through fashion, which really stood out as I played through three of Stranger Than Heaven's eras, with Makoto sporting a different hairstyle and clothes in each one. I also received an answer from art director Daishi Kanaya on these fashion choices, and why, unlike recent Yakuza games, the player won't have free rein to customise them.

Recent findings suggest that "Rather than simply incorporating the fashions of the time, we wanted Makoto’s appearance and clothing to convey his position and situation in life, the relationships around him, and the environment he is living in at that point in the story - for example, what kind of organisation he belongs to and how much financial security he has," Kanaya explains. "We have not made his appearance customisable by the player. We felt it was important for us to present the version of Makoto that is most appropriate to each stage of his life, so that players can more strongly experience his journey as a person.".

Stranger Than Heaven's ambitions are also evident in the technical advances made with RGG Studio's decade-old in-house Dragon Engine. While recent games have been made as cross-platform releases, this one is coming exclusively to current-gen, which has allowed the studio to incorporate more complex human behaviour to make the world feel more alive, and to use advanced post-processing and lighting to elevate the visuals. This is especially great during the game's lengthy cutscenes, something the studio already prides itself on doing, which also show its flair and understanding of drama, as these aren't just reserved for bombastic action sequences but really shine during quiet human moments, such as Makoto's first meeting with Tae, played exquisitely by Shogun's Moeka Hoshi.

Recent findings suggest that however, Abe clarifies that he also worked closely with Kanaya to develop a distinct visual style that wasn't just about high-fidelity photorealism. "Kanaya has a background in oil painting, while I come from a filmmaking background, so we brought our respective perspectives together as we searched for a visual identity unique to this title," he explains. "We studied vintage lenses, old films, record covers, and paintings from the period, trying to understand what made those works feel so distinctive - the way they captured light, the softness of their focus, and the texture they created.".

Recent findings suggest that as a newly introduced game that sets itself apart from the Yakuza series, even if it's still technically in the same universe, portraying what will be the origins of the Tojo Clan, Stranger Than Heaven has been built from the ground up, a change from the studio's approach to efficiently recycling assets for its successive Yakuza titles. That includes a radically different, if at times awkward, dual-limbed combat system that I previously grappled with at Gamescom, as well as many more new bespoke animations, including everyday actions like Makoto eating food from a stall or drinking from a fountain.

Industry observers note that "While some motions from previous titles were used as a starting point, they were extensively revised - often to the point that their origins would be unrecognisable. This was necessary because Makoto, his world, and the story surrounding him represent a major departure from our previous games. The way people walk and carry themselves differs from a modern setting, and Makoto’s behaviour and reactions to his environment are specific to his character and era. As a result, we needed to create and adjust the animations accordingly.".

According to recent reports, in the case of the combat system, while I still found it a bit of a struggle, especially against multiple foes, it's also intentional so that you're not just easily smacking down enemies like Yakuza's Kazuma Kiryu with simple but powerful inputs. "We took a lot of inspiration from Japanese yakuza films and found how raw their action can feel," Abe explains. "The characters are not martial arts masters; their fights are often desperate and unrefined. They grab each other’s clothes, struggle at close range, and use whatever is around them. It is not simply a matter of throwing punches and kicks. In these films, violence often carries a real sense of life-or-death tension - it is a matter of killing or being killed. Creating that tension, and allowing players to experience Makoto’s fear, desperation, and gradual growth firsthand, was at the core of our approach to the tone of the combat.".

While a lot of research was carried out to ensure environments were authentic to their time period, the game also carries the disclaimer that it is "in no way a reproduction of actual history", which perhaps also gives it licence to be a little anachronistic, such as having Snoop Dogg rapping a few bars in the title song, which musically also has some hip-hop influences, despite the genre originating in the US in the 1970s outside of Stranger Than Heaven's setting. Snoop himself might also be a bit of a distraction - as has been the controversial casting of the late Tupac Shakur, who wasn't shown during this hands-on - as there's a scene where Orpheus teaches Makoto how to roll his own tobacco (indicative of its time period; smoking in this game actually gives you buffs), though given one of the ingredients is "grass", I couldn't help but be taken out of the moment and think, yep, that's Snoop.

Recent findings suggest that "What mattered to us was depicting a reimagined world and era with a sense of realism to depict what we wanted as a gameplay experience and narrative," Abe explains. "The same approach applied to the casting of Snoop Dogg. Orpheus would teach Makoto how to survive in Japan and how to make money through music and show business, and at the same time, he is a smuggler who brings Makoto from America to Japan. He needed to be someone formidable - someone with musical talent who could also handle emotionally demanding scenes. So from early on, we had the idea that it would be amazing if Snoop Dogg could play the role.".

That still leaves the question of setting a story across a period of Japanese history that, while full of cultural change, is also controversial. Considering that Stranger Than Heaven's story depicts racial discrimination in Japan, I can't help but think of the multigenerational drama Pachinko, also beginning in 1915, depicting the treatment of Korean immigrants in Japan during its imperial rule of Korea, which seems entirely absent. You could also argue that the story intentionally skims over more controversial moments in the country's history, notably omitting the 1930s, when it invaded China, and ending before the civil unrest of the late 1960s.

Ultimately, Abe argues that the focus is more on Makoto's personal journey than on recounting history. "The game does touch on historical events, for example, its 1943 Osaka setting takes place during wartime, but the narrative is fundamentally centred on Makoto Daito’s life rather than depicting history in detail," he explains. "Even during war, which profoundly affects the lives of everyone, people still live their own individual lives, and Makoto is no different.".

Stranger Than Heaven is then as ambitious as it is contentious, but through its Japanese-Western cultural exchanges and a significant upgrade of visuals and systems, it has the potential to be RGG Studio's biggest global hit to date.

Stranger Than Heaven releases on 15 January 2027 for Xbox Series X/S, PS5, and PC.
