Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

📅 31 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people.
  • It has been revealed that but do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne?
  • Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”.

It has been revealed that but do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

Adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more quickly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

It has been revealed that so… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

It has been revealed that which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Industry observers note that adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate upcoming cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

In a recent development, adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Recent findings suggest that research shows that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

According to recent reports, though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Sources indicate that feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

According to recent reports, thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Recent findings suggest that drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

Industry observers note that when you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

Industry observers note that if this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

It has been revealed that as the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Preparing for a Thai massage is simple!

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

In a recent development, your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

It has been revealed that the ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spanish lighting brand Marset has showcased five of its products on Dezeen Showroom, including a mid-century reissue and a ceiling light that appears like a block of ice.

Marset‘s selection includes the Gambosa table lamp, created by designer Mathias Hahn to reinterpret the classic shade, stem and base as one smooth, glossy sculpture in steel and opal polycarbonate.

Industry observers note that gambosa is defined by its elegant composition, with a round-ended body that looks as if precariously balanced. It also features a considered cable design that sweeps down one side of the lamp like a signature.

It is distinguished by its select palette of colours, with combinations of orange, moss grey, black, pale pink and opal that evoke mid-century style combined with contemporary curation.

With the Lauro collection, Marset has revived a genuine 1970s design classic from its own catalogue, featuring chunky tubes of bent steel.

Created by designers P Aragay and J Pérez Mateo, the Lauro lighting comes in table, floor and wall variants. According to Marset, the range represents the technical achievements of a time when bending steel was a huge challenge.

Another of the highlights from Marset is the Ringo lighting, crafted by designer Joan Gaspar from transparent polycarbonate that is rotomoulded, giving it a dimpled texture reminiscent of a melting block of ice.

Available in flush-mounted or pendant styles, the design has a simple cylindrical shape, with scale and materiality bringing fresh life and visual impact.

Another of Gaspar’s designs is Domus, an angular bollard-style outdoor light that, through simple gesture, recalls a warmly lit house at night.

Recent findings suggest that the design is available in three heights. Units can be optionally combined to create a sculptural look and the illusion of multiple windows.

Geometric glass volumes, metal detailing and glowing bar-shaped lighting elements meet in the Fragile collection, designed for the brand by Jaume Ramírez.

The lights come in pendant, wall and table formats, each made up of spherical and conical shades that lend them a playful aesthetic.

The roots of the Marset brand stretch back to the 1940s, when Francisco “Paco” Marset established a small metal foundry in Barcelona.

His grandchildren Javier and Carlos Marset helped reposition the company as the global design brand it is today when they took over in the 1990s, bringing on board designers such as Gaspar, who is a frequent collaborator.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The fact that Cop31 failed to reach a final agreement on tackling climate change is obviously cause for grave concern.
  • “We will not accept a Cop that greenwashes fossil fuel”, declared the EU representative Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, environment and energy, also stating that a climate pact which makes no mention of fossil fuel was “unconscionable” and “failed to meet the moment.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The fact that Cop31 failed to reach a final agreement on tackling climate change is obviously cause for grave concern. Despite the talks in Antalya, Turkey running over by two days as delegates struggled to achieve a consensus, they were ultimately derailed by the refusal by a group of oil producing states—led by Saudi Arabia and including Russia—to allow any mention of fossil fuel in the conference’s final agreement. This despite an agreement already made at Cop28 in 2023 to “transition away” from coal, oil and gas. As a result, more than 130 countries, including the European Union (EU) and the UK, refused to sign off a deal which omitted any reference to the main cause of climate change.

“We will not accept a Cop that greenwashes fossil fuel”, declared the EU representative Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, environment and energy, also stating that a climate pact which makes no mention of fossil fuel was “unconscionable” and “failed to meet the moment.”.

According to recent reports, much of the art on display at Cop also seemed out of kilter with the urgency of the times. The centrepiece of the official CopArt programme, which was installed across the Cop site and curated by art advisor and contemporary art curator Nagihan Ozel, was an extensive installation of 18 mirror panels installed in the Green Zone and created by veteran artist Heinz Mack who has been making similar work since the 1960s. Other conspicuous pieces included Anselm Kiefer’s giant seascape bearing a pair of metal scales, Für Rabbi Löw (2010-12) and a forest made from recycled cardboard from Eva Jospin. Two monumental bronze sculptures by Belgian artist Koen Vanmechelen, one of an ape standing on a mirrored glass sphere balanced on a human thumb and another of a child struggling to hold an iguana, are described by the artist as “exploring our relationship with the natural world.”.

Recent findings suggest that also on show in the Cop Green Zone and an especially jarring symbol of the deep schisms and incompatible agendas that characterised this latest Conference of the Parties were five animal sculptures created from discarded electronic and industrial defence waste materials. These were part of the “Upcycling a Future Vision” art collection launched by Aselsan, Turkey’s largest defence contractor to demonstrate its “commitment to a circular economy”, according to Turkish state-run media, as well as to celebrate the firm’s 50th anniversary and “future of more efficient, innovative and sustainable production.” In a further irony, the defence giant—which is majority owned by the Turkish Armed Forces Foundation and produces electronic warfare technology and naval and air defence missile systems—was awarded a Green Transformation certificate from the Turkish authorities in tribute to its sustainability efforts. These apparently include a five-year road map to maximise energy, water and raw material efficiency whilst reducing carbon emissions and recycling 87% of total waste.

But amidst the chaos and anomalies within Cop some consolation can be gleaned from the fact that, while the oil-producing countries united to derail proceedings (undoubtedly spurred by the absence of an official US delegation and the Trump administration's overt hostility to the global fight to combat climate change), nonetheless 193 countries plus the EU remain committed to the Paris Agreement. Collectively these nations account for around 85% of global emissions. And while not wrapped up in a final deal, a number of significant agreements were made at Cop31 which included countries backing faster electrification and clean energy, drawing up measures to cut methane emissions and passing measures to protect the planet’s forests and oceans and strengthen support for communities impacted by climate change.

In a recent development, beyond the Cop negotiating rooms, there are also glimmers of progress. In the UK greenhouse gas emissions have fallen by more than 50% since 1990 (although this much-vaunted statistic doesn’t include international aviation, shipping and imports and exports, which makes it more like 24%, according to the Office for National Statistics). Solar panels now provide 28% of Pakistan’s power while France and Denmark have revealed roadmaps to phase out all fossil fuel by 2050, with Spain, Portugal and other countries planning to do the same. While these shifts often have as much to do with the fall in the cost of renewable technology and its resilience to market swings as a desire to hit climate goals; nonetheless an incremental frustration at the Cop consensus model means that countries are increasingly going it alone in naming what needs to be done and in identifying how they will tackle it.

Still from The People's Emergency Briefing (2026) featuring naturalist and presenter Chris Packham.

Courtesy National Emergency Briefing.

Recent findings suggest that case in point was last Monday (16 November) when, as Cop31 was rumbling on, an notable milestone was reached in the UK as Parliament debated a nearly 139,000 strong petition which called for the government to hold a UK-wide emergency briefing on the climate and nature crisis. The petition had been generated by the National Emergency Briefing (NEB), a public information campaign consisting of an influential group of leading experts and fronted by the British naturalist and BBC TV presenter Chris Packham. It was asking for a “prime-time Covid-style briefing across all channels” which would be introduced by the Prime Minister and delivered by independent experts in order to spell out the extent and risks posed by climate change and nature loss, along with the action—both public and governmental—that needs to be taken. More than seventy members of parliament from across the political spectrum attended the three-hour debate which ended broadly in favour of the proposed televised emergency briefing, although not officially agreed. Speaking for the government, climate transition minister Katie White MP did go on record to state that she and her colleagues would meet with the leaders of the NEB campaign and “explore opportunities to work together”, and work on public engagement within the government's climate and nature security taskforce.

According to recent reports, just as Westminster was being galvanised by the NEB campaign, so too was the art world. Two days after the briefing debate, Tate Modern hosted a packed screening of The People’s Emergency Briefing, a 50-minute documentary film made by the NEB and presented by Packham. An articulate panel of nine experts starkly presented the urgent threats that climate and nature breakdown pose to food security, nature, the economy, national security and public health. This film, which anyone can freely register to screen, has been responsible for fueling much of the groundswell of both public and parliamentary support for the NEB’s petition. Since its release in April last year, The People’s Emergency Briefing has been shown more than 5000 times across myriad sectors and in venues large and small throughout the UK, from church halls, offices and hospitals, with many more scheduled for the forthcoming months. As Katie White declared at the Parliamentary debate, “a film has become a movement.”.

However—with a few notable exceptions—the People’s Emergency Briefing has not had much airing in the art world. But now this seems set to change thanks to the art world environmental charity the Gallery Climate Coalition (GCC), who organised the screening and the following panel discussion. This was chaired by Frances Morris, the former director of Tate Modern and nowthe GCC's chair, speaking with artist Heather Ackroyd and Peter Lefort, the green futures network manager at the University of Exeter.

The screening of The People's Emergency Briefing at Tate Modern on 18 November 2026.

According to recent reports, among the two-hundred strong audience of artists, including Cornelia Parker and Marcus Coates, academics and art workers from across both the public and commercial sectors, there emerged a strong determination to galvanise action. Many declared a commitment to lobby their MPs, to organise screenings of the People’s Emergency Briefing in their galleries and generally to be more courageous in both acting individually and collectively to help instigate what Peter Lefort compellingly described as “positive tipping points.”.

It has been revealed that as Lefort explained, these tipping points occur when cumulative changes in behaviour, policies, expectations and attitudes reinforce each other and gather momentum to accelerate change and achieve transformative impact. As politicians falter and our systems for joining forces globally become increasingly dysfunctional and inflexible, it now seems increasingly clear that these new forces for change—such as the NEB, with allied activist groups and screenings occuring across Europe—are coming from the grassroots up, and that the creativity of the art world needs to be applied to shift ossified, seemingly intractable structures and open up new ways of thinking.

After all, it was back in 2019 that, on the instigation of artist duo Heather Ackroyd and Dan Harvey, a procession of bell ringing artworkers headed by a woman wearing a coat of living grass and riding a white horse, occupied Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall. The event from the Culture Declares Emergency movement inspired then-director Frances Morris to make the institution of Tate declare a climate and ecological emergency, helping set in motion an increased environmental awareness that is now common currency throughout the art world. In the words of one attendee at last week’s Tate Modern gathering, “we may be small compared to other sectors but we can be LOUD!” So now let’s brush ourselves down after Cop and make our voices heard, before it is too late.

6 Supplements Doctors Actually Take

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that these days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better.
  • Supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise.
  • It has been revealed that still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that these days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better. And you’re not imagining things: Half of adults and one-third of children in the United States take supplements regularly, according to the Office of Dietary Supplements.

Supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise. First, most physicians recommend obtaining nutrients directly from food rather than a pill or capsule. Second, supplements aren’t reviewed for safety and effectiveness by the FDA before they hit shelves. Because of all the concerns surrounding supplements, Jeffrey Linder, MD, MPH, a general internist and professor of medicine at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, takes a dim view of the category overall: In fact, “a vast majority of supplements are probably worthless,” he tells SELF.

It has been revealed that still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different. Many experts, as it turns out, do take some type of supplement, but they are choosy about which ones they select. Read on to learn more about six they actually use.

In a recent development, how it works: Vitamin D plays key roles in bone health and immune function. In fact, low vitamin D is associated with a wide swath of medical conditions, according to Dr. Linder—including cancer, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, and cardiovascular issues (and, famously, seasonal affective disorder, or SAD).

Recent findings suggest that why some docs like it: Vitamin D deficiency is widespread, especially among people who live at northern latitudes that don’t see as much sun during the winter, and people with darker skin. What’s more, few foods contain significant amounts of vitamin D, so it’s tough to source enough from your diet. Lawrence Green, MD, a dermatologist and clinical professor at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, tells SELF that these two factors make vitamin D a rare nutrient “we do need to take supplements for.” Nearly every single one of the eight doctors who spoke with SELF for this article said they take a vitamin D supplement, especially in the winter, though the frequency and dosage varied.

In a recent development, what to keep in mind: Most docs recommend vitamin D3 (also known as cholecalciferol) over vitamin D2 (also known as ergocalciferol), as studies have shown that D3 is more effective at raising vitamin D levels in your blood. Whichever option you decide on, try to take it with food—specifically, an item that contains fat. Because vitamin D is a fat-soluble nutrient, it “absorbs better that way,” Sara Velayati, MD, an obesity medicine specialist at Montefiore Einstein and an assistant professor at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York City, tells SELF. For this reason, Dr. Green makes a point of taking his supplements with breakfast or dinner. “The fattier and thicker the meal,” the better, he claims.

In a recent development, what it does: Calcium is a mineral that helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth. Women in their 40s approaching menopausal age should make it a particular priority to ensure their intake is adequate, Rachel Pessah-Pollack, MD, an endocrinologist at NYU Langone Health and a clinical professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, tells SELF, as the physical changes that come with perimenopause and menopause can heighten bone loss and downstream health conditions like osteoporosis.

It has been revealed that who takes it: Like the other supplements on this list, calcium is best sourced from your diet, Dr. Pessah-Pollack notes. “But if you’re not able to (I try to get dairy products but often come up short), a supplement is needed.” She takes a combined calcium and vitamin D tablet daily, as vitamin D helps calcium absorb.

Recent findings suggest that how to take it: “The type of calcium supplements you are taking matters,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium carbonate and calcium citrate are the two most common. “Calcium carbonate should be taken with food because it requires gastric acid to be absorbed,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium citrate is an alternative that can be taken with or without food.

Sources indicate that how it works: Magnesium is a mineral that can enhance sleep and muscle recovery. Research has also shown that it’s effective at preventing migraines, Raquel Zemtsov, MD, MPH, a family medicine doctor and assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, tells SELF.

Recent findings suggest that why some docs like it: In addition to Dr. Zemtsov, who takes magnesium to stave off migraine symptoms, Dr. Velayati takes magnesium for the sleep benefits. Likewise, Sheeva Talebian, MD, a reproductive endocrinologist at CCRM Fertility of New York, and Kathleen Jordan, MD, an internal medicine physician and chief medical officer at Midi Health, also turn to it at bedtime to boost their shut-eye.

Sources indicate that what to keep in mind: Some types of magnesium are better tolerated, claims Dr. Velayati—something to note if you’re especially sensitive to side effects. Magnesium glycinate “avoids the gastrointestinal upset caused by magnesium oxides and magnesium citrates,” for example, Dr. Jordan says. Depending on your needs, however, magnesium glycinate might not be the best option: Magnesium oxide is the recommended magnesium type for migraines, so that’s the one Dr. Zemtsov keeps on hand, for example. Taking magnesium with food can also help prevent GI distress, according to Dr. Velayati.

How it works: Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats that are important for cardiovascular health. Common omega-3 supplements include fish oil and krill oil.

Why some docs like it: Dr. Jordan, Dr. Talebian, and Dr. Velayati all take omega-3s. “With their anti-inflammatory properties and association with improved brain health, this is a popular supplement among physicians, myself included,” Dr. Jordan, who takes krill oil, states. Similarly, Dr. Velayati dabbles in fish oil, but takes it selectively. “The right dose really depends on the goal, but I don’t think it’s necessary for everyone,” she says.

In a recent development, what to keep in mind: Fish oil supplements can have a characteristic fishy aftertaste, so it might take some trial and error to find one that works for you (read: doesn’t leave you gagging). What’s more, absorption and bioavailability can be a challenge, according to Dr. Jordan. Because omega-3s, like vitamin D, are fat-soluble, taking fish oil with a meal that contains fat can help skirt this problem. Some claim krill oil doesn’t cause the dreaded aftertaste as much as fish oil, and evidence suggests it’s also better absorbed by the body.

How it works: Iron, a mineral, acts as an essential ingredient in hemoglobin, a protein found in your red blood cells. Without enough iron, your blood won’t be able to carry out its core task of delivering oxygen to organs and tissues, resulting in anemia.

Why some docs like it: Iron deficiency is common in women due to the loss of blood during menstruation every month. “Occasionally, despite trying my hardest to seek out iron-rich foods, I still develop an iron deficiency,” Dr. Zemtsov indicates. When that happens, she takes ferrous gluconate (a particular type of iron supplement) every other day to treat or prevent anemia, since research shows iron supplements are better absorbed and cause fewer side effects that way. Dr. Jordan also takes iron supplements, citing the advantages for sleep, hair health, and overall energy.

According to recent reports, what to keep in mind: Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C, so pairing your iron supplement with a food that contains vitamin C or even a vitamin C supplement—as Dr. Zemtsov does—can be helpful.

Industry observers note that how it works: Fiber, a type of carb, boosts digestion in a variety of ways: It keeps you full, helps prevent constipation, and supports bowel health. Besides the GI stuff, it also serves other functions in your body, including stabilizing your blood sugar and lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol.

Industry observers note that why some docs like it: “Unless you are that rare woman who regularly gets in her 25 to 30 grams per day, extra fiber intake is beneficial for almost everyone, and addresses multiple issues for me personally, including prediabetes and a rising cholesterol level,” Dr. Jordan says. She takes a fiber supplement as needed, on days when she doesn’t manage to hit her goal.

What to keep in mind: If your body isn’t acclimated to a high fiber intake, suddenly bombarding it could cause some digestive distress (think gas and bloating), so start slow to ease the transition. You’ll also need to increase your water intake simultaneously, since fiber requires water to work.

“When someone is considering a supplement, I usually recommend having a specific reason for taking it”—like a confirmed nutritional deficiency, Dr. Velayati says. “Overall, I view supplements as a way to fill a gap, not a substitute for good nutrition, sleep, exercise, and evidence-based medical care.” The bottom line: Supplements are really meant for plugging holes in your diet.

Industry observers note that looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

Recent findings suggest that the nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.).

Nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Recent findings suggest that science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

In a recent development, almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

Older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

Since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

Research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

In 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

Showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

According to recent reports, whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s important to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

Industry observers note that you can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:.

If you’re fresh to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

Sources indicate that don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

Argentina leads the way in repatriating Indigenous human remains, study indicates

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Driven largely by Indigenous activism, the repatriation of ancestral human remains in Chile and Argentina is pushing museums, universities and scientific institutions to re-examine longstanding practices of collection, research and display.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Argentina is central to any discussion of this glitch in South America, since it is the first country in the region with a law specifically aimed at the restitution of Indigenous human remains,” Ayala, an archaeologist at the Universidad de Chile, Santiago tells The Art Newspaper.
  • The researchers’ article, “Indigenous Repatriation Movements in South America and Their Repercussions on Ethical Discussions on the Respectful Treatment of Human Remains: The Cases of Chile and Argentina”, was published on 11 September in the journal Latin American Antiquity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Driven largely by Indigenous activism, the repatriation of ancestral human remains in Chile and Argentina is pushing museums, universities and scientific institutions to re-examine longstanding practices of collection, research and display. A recent study by the Chilean researchers Jacinta Arthur and Patricia Ayala suggests that the movement has opened a crucial ethical debate in both countries, with key differences: while Chile has handled repatriation campaigns on a case-by-case basis, Argentina has emerged as a regional leader since passing a law specifically tackling the glitch.

Recent findings suggest that “Argentina is central to any discussion of this glitch in South America, since it is the first country in the region with a law specifically aimed at the restitution of Indigenous human remains,” Ayala, an archaeologist at the Universidad de Chile, Santiago tells The Art Newspaper. “In Chile, by contrast, there is no legal framework of this kind. That is why it was both necessary and interesting to compare the two realities.”.

The researchers’ article, “Indigenous Repatriation Movements in South America and Their Repercussions on Ethical Discussions on the Respectful Treatment of Human Remains: The Cases of Chile and Argentina”, was published on 11 September in the journal Latin American Antiquity. It emerged from Arthur and Ayala’s work with Indigenous communities in Chile, particularly the campaigns led by the Atacameño and Rapa Nui people, where demands for the respectful treatment of human remains include critiques of their scientific study, museum display, sample collection, repatriation and reburial.

Those efforts were underscored last July, when the Australian Museum in Sydney returned the remains of ancestors of the Rapa Nui people who had been removed from sacred burial sites at Rano Raraku during a German naval expedition in 1882, and acquired by the museum the following year. The institution’s director, Kim McKay, publicly acknowledged the circumstances under which the ancestors’ remains had entered the collection, and said: “Returning them is an act of moral responsibility.”.

It has been revealed that according to Ayala, despite the legal differences between Argentina and Chile, the treatment of human remains from an Indigenous perspective “has not yet become central to scientific concerns”. Indigenous activism, she indicates, has forced museums and archaeologists to confront “the exclusion of Indigenous voices” and “alternative knowledge and ontologies” linked to ancestral bodies and the materials associated with them. It has also brought renewed attention to the violence of looting, collecting and scientific research that helped shape colonial and national museums, where Indigenous ancestral remains have ended up since at least the 19th century.

“In this context, both museums and academic fields have begun to reflect on their practices and discourses,” Ayala says, “although much work remains to be done to fully integrate the rights of Indigenous peoples in both countries.”.

Argentina passed a law in 2001 mandating that Indigenous human remains held in public or private collections must be made available to the peoples or communities that claim them. An implementing decree followed in 2010, making the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs responsible for surveying and identifying remains, and coordinating their return.

Recent findings suggest that A recent case at the Museo Etnográfico Juan B. Ambrosetti, part of the Universidad de Buenos Aires, reveals how such restitutions unfold in practice. Last May the museum returned the remains of an Inca child from Apu Chañi, along with his grave goods, to El Angosto and Sol de Mayo, two communities in the El Moreno area of Jujuy state. The child had entered the museum’s collection in 1905, after being brought down from a hill on Nevado de Chañi. Following the restitution, a mausoleum was built at the foot of the mountain to display the grave goods, while the child’s remains will be buried at high altitude when conditions in the freezing high Andes allow.

“What I think is missing here, above all, is getting ahead of restitutions, not waiting for communities to file a claim,” Andrea Pegoraro, the director of the Museo Etnográfico, tells The Art Newspaper. Pegoraro, says the return of the child from Apu Chañi reveals that Argentina has a more developed legal framework than many neighbouring countries, but also exposes the limits of a policy based solely on responding to claims.

According to recent reports, that, she states, is one of the challenges still facing Argentine museums: moving from responding to specific requests to actively reviewing collections, identifying provenance gaps, reconstructing acquisition histories and contacting the relevant communities. In the Apu Chañi case, she says, the museum reviewed archival and archaeological records to establish where the remains had been taken and to which community they should be returned.

Industry observers note that at the restitution ceremony, Pegoraro said the museum was not handing over “a heritage object or an object of study”, but rather “an ancestor to his territory and his people”. The community, in turn, described the returned ancestor as “a guardian” connected to water and life in the Puna region of Jujuy.

For Pegoraro, the distinction between human remains and objects is crucial. “If they are human remains, I am fully in favour of returning them, and the community must decide what to do with them,” she notes. Objects raise a different set of considerations, in her view: to whom they should be returned, what happens to them and how museums can ensure access for other communities.

According to recent reports, reconstructing provenance is essential to any restitution process, Pegoraro adds, because Indigenous territories do not always align with today’s political boundaries. “Communities inhabit territories that did not previously have the political or geographical boundaries we have today,” she says. Museums often rely on documentation archaeologists wrote at the time the remains entered a collection, even when the places they recorded no longer correspond neatly to current jurisdictions.

Pegoraro also warns that change cannot be limited to isolated restitutions. “The integration of Indigenous communities does not come only through rhetoric, or by carrying out a restitution or holding an exhibition once in a while, but by literally working side by side,” she says. She adds that collaboration must include the ongoing rewriting of exhibition narratives, as well as financial compensation.

In Pegoraro’s view, the current movement for repatriation of Indigenous remains and artefacts began in the 1980s, especially in the US, Australia, Newly introduced Zealand and Canada. In Argentina and elsewhere in South America, she adds, those demands gained force with the return of democracy after dictatorships. In Europe, however, museums carry “a much stronger colonial history”, she indicates, and while some countries are beginning to talk about decolonising collections, returning objects or rewriting narratives, “they still have a long way to go. It must not remain just rhetoric.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, at some point in most women’s lives, a familiar line of thinking creeps in—whether on its own or planted by well-meaning parents: What if I don’t get married? What if I never find my person and end up alone?

It has been revealed that for Joan, the panic hit in her 30s—strong enough to land her in a psychologist’s office. Back then, she says, “a woman who didn’t want a husband was assumed to have something wrong with her.” But her therapist—married with children, yet more open-minded than most—didn’t try to correct her with cheesy motivational mantras or fear tactics about a “ticking clock.” Instead, she asked a different question: What kind of husband would you want, if you had one?

In a recent development, joan listed a few traits. Someone busy, she recalls saying. Someone deeply absorbed in his own life—his job, his hobbies, his community.

“So you'd want someone intellectually stimulating?” her therapist asked.

“No,” Joan replied. “I’d want someone who’s never home.”.

It landed as a joke, though deep down, it wasn’t. What came from that session was an almost accidental realization that sounded radical at the time (it was around 1980): “Some people genuinely live their best lives independently,” Joan tells me. Now 79, single, and uninterested in changing her relationship status, she has spent decades proving her theory true.

For much of modern history, women like Joan were cast as anomalies, freaks, or worse: cautionary tales. There’s “the childless cat lady.” The “old maid.” The “lonely spinster.” Singlehood was framed as a transitional phase, a temporary stop on the way to finding the One. Not an end goal, and certainly not a fulfilling one.

But the stigma is softening—and the older, unmarried women of this generation are living proof that a life without a husband isn’t a fallback; it’s a deeply satisfying choice.

You can see it in the collective fatigue around modern dating (78% of people on apps including Tinder, Hinge, and Bumble reported feeling burnt out, per a recent Forbes Health survey). Young adults in their mid 20s to early 30s (the supposed “prime marriage years”) are having far less sex than previous generations, with sexual inactivity up roughly 50% for women over the past decade. The shift demonstrates up in pop culture too—in particular, the growing appetite for plots that sideline romance in favor of friendship, independence, and chosen families (like in Barbie and Wicked).

Industry observers note that but perhaps the clearest proof is in lived experiences. The several 70-somethings I spoke with for this story have been single for decades—and aren’t wishing they’d done it any differently. If anything, their lives carry a sense of ease and expansiveness. Many describe weekly, laughter-filled girls’ nights and happy hours; solo trips planned on a whim; financial freedom to buy property, adopt pets, start small businesses…literally do whatever they want, whenever they want. A few still date casually, dipping in and out of steamy flings only when it suits them. Others have opted out of romance entirely. “My favorite part?” one 73-year-old woman tells me bluntly. “Not having to bicker or put up with an incompetent man. That’s probably why I’m the least stressed I’ve ever been.”.

Across their stories, there’s no regret or hint of “missing out.” Just single older ladies enjoying where they are—nothing like the caricatures of the bitter man-hater or the desperate, unlucky romantic we’re used to seeing.

Sources indicate that as Joan is quick to point out, “not everyone starts off wanting a romantic relationship and then moves on to singlehood as Plan B.” It’s a perspective that’s become increasingly common, so much so that sociologist Bella DePaulo, PhD, built a framework (and wrote a book) about it: being Single at Heart. These are women (including herself) who don’t end up alone; they orient toward it as a genuine preference.

“I still smile when I think about the men I dated when I was a very young adult,” Dr. DePaulo, 72, tells me. “But I remember even more fondly how I felt when each of those relationships ended: finally free.”.

The practical benefits of singledom—solitude, strong friendships, fewer relational stressors—aren’t exclusive to unmarried folks. “But in my opinion, couples are never free the way single people are,” Dr. DePaulo notes. The difference, she claims, is psychological: the ability to structure a day, a life, or a passing thought without reflexively factoring in another person’s needs or reactions. “A romantic partner is also there in your mind almost all the time,” Dr. DePaulo points out—even if only on the periphery. “That might be comforting for some. But it can also feel a bit unwelcome, as if they’re always considering what their significant other may be wanting or feeling.” Remove that, and your attention and energy become fully your own.

It has been revealed that of course, the ability to choose this lifestyle is relatively recent. For centuries, marriage wasn’t just a matter of romance—women relied on it for financial stability, social acceptance, and a sanctioned path to family, Kris Marsh, PhD, sociologist and author of The Love Jones Cohort: Single and Living Alone in the Black Middle Class, tells SELF. But with greater access to education, careers, and economic independence (along with broader definitions of intimacy, family, and fulfillment), the pressure to couple up has eased. As of 2023, 42% of US adults were unpartnered, according to the Pew Research Center (up from 29% in 1990). And among the non-daters younger than 50, half aren’t interested in a relationship—though enjoying your single status doesn’t have to involve an anti-love attitude.

“Now, a lot of women are looking for something additive,” Dr. Marsh notes. “I’ve heard over and over, ‘I’m already in a very good place on my own. So you can’t be a distraction. You can’t disrupt my peace.’” Though for most, that epiphany doesn’t happen overnight.

In a recent development, alice Foster, who recently turned 80, is a classic example of someone who followed the cultural script handed to many in her generation: marry young, raise children, enjoy the stability. “It was fine, but I felt like it was never really about me,” Foster tells SELF. “It wasn’t my life.”.

Sources indicate that in 1988, her marriage ended in divorce—though what followed wasn’t the loss she had been taught to fear. It was space. Peace. Recalibration. She moved upstate. Went back to school. Built a upcoming career in nursing. Slowly, she began constructing a life that finally felt like her own.

Recent findings suggest that “I feel like I’m in my 50s. It’s been so fun,” she reflects. “I love being retired. I love traveling. I love having people visit me. I love not having to answer to anybody. I’ve been single for so long and loving this life so much that, honestly, I don’t want to get tied down.” And that, experts say, is often how it works.

Rather than being a fixed moral stance or a lifelong rejection of romance, singlehood tends to be a lived, flexible experience—an acceptance of being on your own that you don’t always realize you’re choosing until later. Maybe, like Foster, you leave an unsatisfying marriage. You pull back on exhaustive online dating. You decide this is the year you’ll focus on work, hobbies, or travel. Over time, you stop planning life around the possibility of a relationship…and start seeing that you already have the joy you thought only a husband could provide.

Still, a question tends to linger: Are these women actually happy?

Industry observers note that recent research suggests yes—in fact, satisfaction with singlehood tends to increase with age, starting for people in their 40s. Despite cultural progress, there’s still skepticism as to why anyone would willingly stay single. Whereas married people are taken at their word when they claim fulfillment (even though we know that’s not always true), those who deviate face public scrutiny. “They have to be extra strong, exceptionally confident to stand comfortably in their singleness and validate to the world that they are, in fact, thriving,” Dr. Marsh adds—an expectation that flattens single older ladies into either a hyper-independent success story or a pitiable failure, with little room for nuance.

According to recent reports, but that pressure can have an unintended effect too. After decades of being asked by society to justify their lifestyle, many simply stop performing. All of the women I spoke with didn’t overexplain. They weren’t defensive. They didn’t seem especially interested in winning me over.

It takes a certain kind of confidence and clarity to stop shaping your life around what’s expected and historically rewarded, and instead follow what feels good, without apology. What you get then, as Dr. Marsh has observed in her research, is a quieter, rarer form of happiness—one that isn’t performed and doesn’t ask for external validation. Instead, it feels much more genuine. It endures.

Sources indicate that so, what’s the deal with 4A hair? 4A hair is the queen of the fine, loose curl pattern. It forms tight, springy coils that are like tiny, perfect S-shapes. These curls are less dense than their 4B and 4C cousins, making them more defined and delicate. Think of 4A hair as the Goldilocks of coily hair — not too tight, not too loose, but just right.

Industry observers note that your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:.

4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. Keeping it moisturized is essential, so incorporate a good leave-in conditioner into your daily shampooing routine. Use deep conditioning treatments weekly to replenish moisture and strengthen your curls.

Don’t forget scalp care, too! For maximum hydration, look for products with ingredients like shea butter, coconut oil, and glycerin.

Sources indicate that 4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

According to recent reports, heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

It has been revealed that protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai.

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

It has been revealed that regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

Sources indicate that to determine your hair type, look at the curl pattern, texture, and density. 4A hair has a loose curl pattern with fine, springy coils, while 4B and 4C hair have tighter curls. 3C hair is curly but not as tight as Type 4.

Washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

  • In a recent development, you might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Industry observers note that most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going. If that balance consistently feels off—not just once or twice, but over the course of weeks or months—it’s hard not to wonder whether something deeper is going on.

In a recent development, you might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation. They call, if at all, only when they’re bored or when it’s convenient. And then there’s the sharper sting of noticing how effortlessly they find time for other people—just not for you (a surprisingly common frustration you can read more about here).

It has been revealed that to be fair, life can get in the way—people get busy, schedules clash, and our friends can’t always be as available as we’d like—but that doesn’t make it any less frustrating or stop you from feeling resentful when you’re waiting days for a simple “How are you?” But how do you know if this is a temporary lapse or a more unhealthy one-sided friendship? Here are the biggest red flags therapists want you to watch out for.

Industry observers note that look through your texts and DMs: Are you always the first to send a message? When’s the last time they suggested hanging out? You can also experiment by not reaching out to see how long it takes for them to initiate contact. If weeks (or months) go by without a word, their silence may indicate who’s really holding this connection together.

“At a minimum, a good friend (even a busy one) will periodically check in out of curiosity and interest,” Tiana Leeds, LMFT, a therapist based in Santa Barbara, California, tells SELF. After all, someone who truly cares about you should want to know what’s going on in your life, which is why if they consistently don’t try to get in touch (or only expect you to do so), they may not be genuinely interested in your world.

Venting to your friends is natural—some would even argue it can strengthen your bond. That said, being there for each other is supposed to be a two-way street, Hope Kelaher, LCSW, author of Here to Make Friends: How to Make Friends as an Adult, tells SELF.

If someone unloads their laundry list of problems but doesn’t listen to yours, “they’re likely using you as their on-call therapist,” Kelaher claims. This one-directional dynamic could look like a person who constantly complains about their boss but changes the subject whenever you open up about your work-related stress. Or they dominate dinner conversations with their dating disasters, yet they’re “busy,” uninterested, or MIA when you need relationship advice. Over time, investing all your time and energy into people who won’t give back can drain your energy, Leeds says, and leave you feeling neglected by a person who’s supposed to have your back.

In a recent development, maybe they insist on eating at restaurants near their place, which means you have to travel across town every single time. They only reach out when “better” aims fall through (“Hey, my dinner got canceled. What are you doing tonight?”), making you feel more like an afterthought than a priority. More subtly, perhaps they’re only interested in brief 15-minute coffee chats that fit their schedule instead of a dedicated dinner or movie night.

According to recent reports, “In a healthy relationship there should always be a give-and-take,” Kelaher states, meaning both people need to compromise. So it’s disheartening when, again and again, someone you’d do anything for won’t meet you halfway (sometimes literally).

Your friend might be a workaholic or chronically forgetful (which, don’t get us wrong, is still frustrating). But that alone doesn’t mean your bond is one-sided.

Instead, “consider the bigger picture and ask yourself, ‘Is their behavior a reflection of not caring about me, or just a difference in availability and communication style?’” Leeds says. As an example, someone who takes five business days to reply to anyone’s messages may not be singling you out. What’s more telling, though, is if that same person who’s “too swamped” to text you regularly posts Instagram stories of brunches, dinners, and post-work meetups with others in their social circle. Or if your usually punctual friend (who’s known for being reliable) is comfortable canceling plans only with you. These inconsistencies, Kelaher says, suggest that they’re perfectly capable of showing up—just not for you.

Let’s say you mentioned how notable it would be to have support at your first 5K race. A friend who truly cares might surprise you at the finish line with flowers, or at the very least shoot over a heartfelt “Good luck!” or “Congrats!” In a one-sided friendship, however, this kind of consideration may be missing entirely. They might downplay your achievement (“Sorry I couldn’t make it, but it was such a short race!”) or forget your big day without a hint of apology.

Recent findings suggest that true friends go the extra mile to celebrate your successes and be there during tough moments. That’s why if someone repeatedly forgets significant events like your birthday, or rarely highlights empathy for your challenges (like a scary medical procedure, a high-stakes presentation), they may not be as invested as they should be.

Therapists recommended bringing up your concerns non-confrontationally.

Recent findings suggest that ideally, their response can give you a glimpse into whether they’re aware of this imbalance and, more importantly, if they’re willing to work on it. That stated, you can’t force someone to be a good friend, so if they don’t care enough to show up for you, know that you deserve better. “After all, friendships take work, Leeds says. “But it’s not meant to be done by just one person.”.

Pucker Up! How to Heal Cracked Lip Corners Fast

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful!
  • It has been revealed that the first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture.
  • Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

It has been revealed that the first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Recent findings suggest that locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

In a recent development, have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

In a recent development, it might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”.

Recent findings suggest that whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Recent findings suggest that also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will swiftly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

In a recent development, if your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

According to recent reports, you might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

Say goodbye to painful cracked lip corners in about a week with these easy tips:.

Talk to a dermatologist for customized care if your lip corners become red, swollen, or more painful after a few days.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that denver Design District has unveiled a slick new brand identity, transforming the once exclusive design commerce hub into a fresh cultural destination. A blend of design-focused goods, art, retail and food, the new identity marks a more accessible, culturally relevant district made for the masses.

While there's no formula for creating the best rebrands, Denver Design District's latest identity shines in its attention to detail, honouring its rich design heritage while embracing a newfound playfulness. Sleek, timeless and characterful, the new brand identity is the ultimate love letter to design.

Recent findings suggest that created in collaboration with D4 Urban and design studio Wunder Werkz, the Denver Design District rebrand centres around a wonderfully contemporary brandmark. Representing the district's evolution, the 3 'Ds' motif compresses the bold letterforms by a third each time, making for a dynamic visual anchor.

Industry observers note that to accomodate the brandmark, Wunder Werkz created DDD Standard, a bespoke midweight sans serif, to act as the district's display typeface. Equal parts "architectural and playful", it draws inspiration from Herbert Bayer's mid-century furniture forms. Paired with an iconographic system of silhouetted design products, clarity and cohesion flow throughout the identity with a confident authority.

Sources indicate that “The idea was to make a more welcoming, accessible district; one that celebrates design in all its forms,” explains Jon Hartman, Partner at Wunder Werkz. “Trade remains an important part of the ecosystem, but it is no longer the whole story. So, we needed to design a brand that felt open and culturally relevant while still carrying the credibility of the design industry.”.

It has been revealed that A rich colour system of brick, blush, slate and deep yellow contrasts the tans and greys of the district's buildings, bringing warmth and personality to the clean design. The result is a refined homage to design that feels accessible and unpretentious, without losing the slick essence of the design district.

“This project represents the kind of work we love most because it allows us to engage at every level, from strategy and stakeholder alignment through implementation and installation,” adds Hartman. “For us, that’s where the best work happens. Not when design is treated as an afterthought, but when it becomes the link between strategy, space and experience. The result is a brand that feels cohesive at every scale, from a website headline to a warehouse-sized building facade.”.

Industry observers note that “Denver Design District has always been rooted in great design, but our vision for its future is much broader,” says Dan Cohen, CEO of Denver Design District. “This rebrand isn’t about changing who we are, it’s about reflecting what the District is becoming: a more dynamic, connected, and welcoming destination for Denver and the entire Rocky Mountain region.”.

For more creative inspiration, check out The Royal Albert Hall's majestic rebrand or take a look at the gorgeous McMichael rebrand that's a pure work of art.

#161512. Tech Report: Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

📅 13 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (979 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago.
  • Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not latest, though it is gaining in popularity.
  • Over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—massive and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not latest, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

Over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

For some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

Sources indicate that “It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” says Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

Recent findings suggest that patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting upcoming collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is promptly becoming the preferred method.

It has been revealed that “[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” indicates Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

Recent findings suggest that this type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” says Dr. Pearl.

Dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

Industry observers note that while there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

This is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

Try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

For cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

Recent findings suggest that but will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” indicates Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

If you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

In a recent development, if injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a plan to minimize your pain.
